title-group.article-title: Charging Rate and Storage Capacity Tradeoffs in Composite Cold Thermal Energy Storage for Sustainable Cooling

abstract.p: Cold thermal energy storage supports sustainable cooling by separating cold production from demand, while conductive additives alter both charging performance and material requirements. This study investigates how ternary particles and a copper network affect freezing time, retained latent capacity, and composite mass in a wavy-walled water-based storage cell with two cooled fins. A conservative finite-volume enthalpy model was used to evaluate 12 combinations of TiO$_2$–Ag–Al$_2$O$_3$ particle loading and porosity. Numerical verification included comparison with a two-phase Stefan solution and refinement of the spatial grid, time step, and phase-change temperature interval. Skeleton-conductance sensitivity was also assessed. Under the nominal conditions, the times to reach a mean solid fraction of 0.99 were 64.92 s for water, 55.95 s for particles alone, 15.14 s for foam alone, and 14.12 s for the combined medium. The combined configuration shortened freezing by 78.25%, retained 90.73% of the water-baseline volumetric latent capacity, and achieved an average latent charging index 4.17 times the baseline value. Adding particles to the foam shortened freezing by a further 6.76%; however, the foam-only medium stored more latent cooling after 10 s, at 273.92 versus 268.29 MJ$\cdot$m$^{-3}$. At equal full latent capacity, the combined medium required 10.22% more material volume and 78.78% more composite mass than water. These findings identify charging deadlines and required storage capacity as joint criteria for conductive-material allocation. The analysis provides a quantitative basis for balancing charging performance and material requirements in cold thermal energy storage for sustainable cooling.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Cold thermal energy storage separates cooling production from cooling demand. Its value depends on both the amount of cooling retained and the time needed to establish that inventory. A store that freezes within a short production window can be scheduled differently from one that requires prolonged refrigeration. Reviews of cold-storage control and materials therefore connect transient thermal performance with equipment operation and the timing of electricity use [1], [2], [3]. For sustainable cooling, this connection makes charging duration and resource allocation complementary design variables.

Water offers a large latent heat near a temperature useful for ice storage. During charging, heat must travel from the remaining liquid through a growing solid region to the cooled surfaces. A substantial latent capacity can consequently coexist with a long freezing period. Experiments and numerical studies of building cooling stores, together with discharge assessments, distinguish the stored inventory from its rate of access [4], [5]. The material and geometry selected for a store should therefore be evaluated against the available charging period as well as its eventual cooling duty.

Thermal transport can be modified through dispersed particles, extended surfaces, and conductive porous structures [6], [7], [8]. These measures act differently. Nanoparticles change the effective properties of the phase-changing medium, whereas fins and metal foam extend conductive paths into the enclosure. A recent review of foam–phase change composites emphasizes the dependence on structural parameters and the thermal model used to represent them [9]. Effective-conductivity studies connect that dependence to network topology and to the correlation used for the composite medium [10], [11]. Conductive additions also occupy space and contribute mass, so their charging response must be considered alongside the retained phase-changing material.

Fin–foam cold-storage studies examine how conductive paths intersect regions of residual liquid [12]. Related work addresses melting in fin–foam structures, solidification with branch-shaped fins and nanoparticles, and composite media in triplex-tube heat exchangers [13], [14], [15]. Investigations covering complete melting–solidification cycles and experimentally assessed fin–foam arrangements show why performance must be interpreted within the chosen geometry and thermal boundary conditions [16], [17]. Ice-storage experiments with copper foam and studies of partial filling further identify the distribution of metal as a design variable [18], [19]. Cycle-level investigations extend this question to the charging and discharging sequence [20].

Particle-containing media introduce a second material allocation. Experiments with graphene-based water suspensions and functionalized graphene–CuO mixtures assess stability and phase-change behavior alongside thermal transport [21], [22]. Studies of other nanocomposite storage materials and TiO
2
–Ag dispersions similarly connect composition with thermal properties and stability [23], [24]. Thermophysical compilations for ternary mixtures provide constituent-property inputs for multicomponent media [25]. For storage design, the volume occupied by particles also changes the amount of water available to freeze, while the density of the particles changes capacity per unit composite mass.

Combined particle and foam arrangements already have relevant precedents. Mirparizi investigated ternary particles and metal foam in cold storage [26], and Shafee considered a wavy-walled enclosure with internal fins and a porous ternary medium [27]. Studies of radiative finned storage, nanoparticle-assisted freezing, and tree-finned composite enclosures provide further comparisons [28], [29], [30]. These precedents establish the thermal mechanism of combined conductive measures. The remaining design question addressed here is how the separate and joint material additions compare when freezing time, latent inventory, composite mass, and a finite charging deadline are evaluated on the same basis.

The present study defines a two-dimensional conduction benchmark with a wavy wall, two cooled internal fins, water, equal-volume TiO
2
–Ag–Al
2
O
3
particles, and a copper skeleton. A four-by-three matrix of total particle fraction and porosity separates particle addition from foam incorporation. A foam-only control completes the comparison between the four endpoint material states. A conservative enthalpy calculation is checked against a two-phase Stefan solution and examined through mesh, time-step, and phase-interval refinement. The resulting fields and response measures are then used to evaluate material allocation for scheduled cooling production. The analysis resolves three related design choices: the incremental value of particles after a copper network is installed, the composition that establishes the largest latent inventory by a fixed deadline, and the volume and mass required to retain a specified latent capacity. Skeleton-conductance sensitivity establishes how these comparisons depend on the effective-network representation.

sec.title: 2.4. Spatial discretization and nonlinear solution
sec.p:
The equations are discretized by a cell-centered finite-volume method on a uniform Cartesian grid. The wavy wall and the fin slots are represented by the active-cell mask. Internal face conductivities use harmonic averaging. The prescribed-temperature wall and fin faces use the half-cell distance to the boundary; adiabatic faces contribute zero heat flux. Every internal face contributes equal and opposite heat exchange to its neighboring cells. Equation (8) gives the control-volume update, where
G f
is the face conductance and
V i
is the cell volume per unit out-of-plane depth.

The enthalpy difference is evaluated at the new temperature, and face conductivities are evaluated from the preceding time level. This semi-implicit treatment gives a nonlinear enthalpy solve at each step while retaining the same face fluxes in the heat balance. A damped Newton iteration uses the exact piecewise derivative of enthalpy. Sparse linear systems are solved directly, and a residual-based line search selects the Newton step. The maximum local residual divided by
Λ
must be below 10
− 10
. The implementation permits up to 60 iterations and halves the step following an unsuccessful solve.

The nominal grid has 96 cells along the height, giving
Δ x
=
Δ y
= 62.5 μm. The nominal time step is 0.05 s. Mesh tests use 64, 96, 128, and 192 cells along the height. Time-step tests use 0.10, 0.05, 0.025, and 0.0125 s; phase-interval tests use 0.20, 0.10, and 0.05 K. The two endpoint materials are examined separately. Fin thickness and position coincide with grid faces for all four tested meshes. The changing Cartesian representation of the curved wall is included in the mesh comparison.

Cumulative heat extraction is calculated from the same boundary-face fluxes used in the update. It is compared with the volume integral of the enthalpy decrease at every recorded time. The reported energy residual is their absolute difference divided by the enthalpy decrease. This is a discrete conservation check, complementary to the independent analytical comparison in Section 3.1. The supplementary material contains the solver, all input settings, numerical outputs, and figure scripts.

sec.title: 3.1. Two-phase stefan comparison
sec.p:
A one-dimensional freezing problem provides an independent check on the enthalpy implementation. The rod is 10 mm long, starts at 274.15 K, and has a left boundary at 268.15 K. The far boundary is insulated. Pure-water properties from Table 2 are used, with a 0.05 K phase interval. The analytical semi-infinite two-phase solution gives the interface position in Eq. (11). The positive parameter
λ
satisfies the Stefan heat balance in Eq. (12), where erf and erfcx are the error function and the scaled complementary error function. The interface remains well separated from the far boundary over the 20 s comparison period.

Calculations used 300, 600, and 1200 cells with a 0.01 s time step. The numerical front was obtained by interpolating the $T
=
T_m$ crossing. For the 1200-cell calculation, the largest sampled front-position error over 1–20 s was 2.41%, and the error at 20 s was 0.22%. Table 3 reports every sampled time for this mesh. Figure 2 compares the three numerical resolutions with the analytical front and shows the temperature profile at 20 s. The analytical test checks the moving phase boundary and the temperature field, while the energy residual checks the discrete heat balance.

The foam-only control separates the two material mechanisms. Adding foam to the particle-containing medium reduced its

sec.title: 4.2. Phase-front and temperature development
sec.p: Figure 4 and Figure 5 present the solid fraction and temperature at the same three times for all four endpoint materials. At 5 s, freezing has progressed from the cooled wall and the two fin surfaces, leaving liquid toward the wavy boundary and within thermally remote parts of the cell. The foam-containing materials show a more advanced front at this early stage. The two fields are linked by the same phase relation, so the residual liquid corresponds to temperatures close to the phase-change interval.

caption.title: Solid-fraction distributions for the four endpoint materials
Temperature distributions for the four endpoint materials

sec.p: By 20 s, both foam-containing cases have passed the 99% endpoint, while the foam-free media retain a larger liquid region. At 60 s, the particle-only medium has passed its endpoint and water is close to completing the transition. Temperature continues to fall after the latent transition as the solid composite approaches the cooled-boundary temperature. Comparing the fields at common times therefore reveals both the phase-change advance and the subsequent sensible cooling.

The transient responses in Figure 6 show that the copper network accelerates both phase conversion and subsequent sensible cooling. Once solidification is complete, the mean temperature continues toward the cooled-wall temperature while the latent inventory reaches a composition-dependent plateau. Water retains the largest final latent inventory because it occupies the full storage-region volume.

sec.title: 5.1. Conductive allocation and the choice of design objective
sec.p: The foam-only control isolates the incremental effect of particles after the main conductive network has been established. At fixed porosity, particle addition changes both the pore-medium conductivity and the latent inventory, so its value depends on the charging deadline and the required cooling capacity. Studies of fin–foam and partially filled structures likewise treat the location and quantity of metal as design variables [12], [16], [17], [19]. The present matrix extends that material-allocation question by reporting the same endpoint, capacity basis, and charging deadlines for each composition.

At
γ
= 0.95, adding
ϕ
= 0.045 particles increases
P
99
by 2.42% relative to foam alone, while the mass-specific latent capacity falls from 226.7 to 186.6 kJ
⋅
kg
− 1
. The additional particle loading is therefore a comparatively small rate adjustment in a medium whose main conductive path is already metallic. This supports assessing particle use against an explicit charging requirement and material inventory, and selecting a loading that matches those requirements. Suspension stability and repeatable phase-change behavior remain relevant material-selection considerations established in experimental storage studies [21], [22], [23], [24].

For equal full latent capacity on a storage-material basis, the combined medium requires 10.22% more volume and 78.78% more composite mass than water. These inventory ratios follow from the capacity values in Table 5 and exclude the cooled fins and external containment. They quantify the material commitment associated with the nominal charging-rate gain.

The finite-window result also clarifies the role of the charging index.
P
99
averages the latent inventory established up to a material-specific completion time. A fixed deadline instead compares inventories after the same operating duration. Both are useful, but their reference periods differ. The higher
P
99
of the combined material and the larger 10 s inventory of the foam-only medium are compatible outcomes of those definitions. Selecting an objective that matches the cooling duty is consequently as important as selecting a conductive composite.

sec.title: 5.2. Relevance to sustainable cooling operation
sec.p: Sustainable cooling requires coordination between cold production, electricity availability, and the cooling load. Control studies place this coordination at system level [1], [2], [3]. The present benchmark supplies component-level quantities for that task: a defined freezing endpoint, a latent inventory as a function of the charging deadline, and material capacity on volume and mass bases. A restricted production period can favor a conductive skeleton, whereas a longer period increases the value of retaining water. These quantities can be passed to a cooling-system calculation with its refrigeration coefficient of performance, storage heat losses, discharge schedule, and electricity profile.

The distinction between charging rate and refrigeration electricity is important for interpreting the engineering contribution. The reference cell imposes a cooled-boundary temperature and resolves the resulting heat transfer. Its sustainability assessment concerns the allocation of phase-changing material and the timing of cold production. System operation determines how that thermal response translates into electricity demand and resource use over repeated cycles. Full-cycle studies of composite stores provide a complementary basis for extending the component comparison to charging and discharge together [16], [20].

sec.title: 5.3. Model scope and extension to storage hardware
sec.p: The calculations define an idealized local-thermal-equilibrium conduction benchmark with cooled fins and temperature-independent constituent inputs. This representation provides a common basis for material comparisons. The skeleton factor explicitly exposes the influence of the assumed network conductance, and the resolution checks quantify the numerical sensitivity of the reference cell. A hardware-specific application can assign effective conductivities from measured foam morphology and contact conditions, introduce the actual heat-transfer-fluid boundary, and examine the resulting full operating cycle. Experimental fin–foam and ice-storage investigations supply relevant configurations for that progression [17], [18].

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p:
This study examined the tradeoff between charging performance and material requirements in a wavy-walled cold thermal energy storage cell containing cooled fins, TiO
2
–Ag–Al
2
O
3
particles, and a copper conductive network. A conservative enthalpy model, verified against a two-phase Stefan solution and assessed through numerical refinement, separated the contributions of particles and foam across 12 material configurations. The comparison established how freezing time, retained latent capacity, and composite mass jointly influence material selection.

The copper network accounted for the dominant reduction in freezing time. Under the nominal conditions, the time to reach a mean solid fraction of 0.99 decreased from 64.92 s for water to 55.95 s with particles, 15.14 s with foam, and 14.12 s with both. The combined configuration reduced freezing time by 78.25% relative to water, whereas adding particles to the foam provided a further reduction of 6.76%. These findings identify network conductance as the primary design variable, with particle loading providing a smaller adjustment once the metallic pathway is established.

Faster phase conversion was accompanied by lower latent capacity and greater material requirements. The combined medium retained 90.73% of the water-baseline volumetric latent capacity and achieved an average latent charging index 4.17 times the baseline value. Its mass-specific latent capacity, however, decreased to 186.6 kJ
⋅
kg
− 1
. At equal full latent capacity, this composition required 10.22% more storage-material volume and 78.78% more composite mass than water. Charging deadlines also changed the preferred configuration: after 10 s, foam alone stored 273.92 MJ
⋅
m
− 3
, exceeding the combined medium’s 268.29 MJ
⋅
m
− 3
despite its longer freezing time. Material selection therefore depends on the cooling inventory required within the available charging period.

For sustainable cooling, these results support allocating conductive material according to both charging constraints and retained storage capacity. A copper network is particularly effective when rapid charging is required, while additional particles should be assessed against their incremental charging gain and associated capacity and mass penalties. The resulting performance measures provide component-level inputs for storage sizing and cooling-production scheduling. Further research should connect morphology-dependent network conductivity with complete charging–discharging cycles and refrigeration-system operation to assess electricity use and material requirements over repeated service.
